An AVS-licensed pet shop is a Singapore business approved by the Animal and Veterinary Service, a unit of the National Parks Board, to keep and sell dogs. Licensing means welfare inspections, mandatory owner-suitability screening, and annual renewal, not just a name on a shopfront. Curious Tails holds AVS pet shop licence AS24J00046. Bringing a Puppy Home to an HDB Flat HDB rules allow one dog of an approved breed, or an approved cross, per flat. Condo and landed property owners can keep up to three, subject to the property's own pet policy. Corgis and Shiba Inus are not on the standard HDB-approved list. We'll tell you this plainly if you're considering either, rather than let you find out after you've already fallen for a puppy. Cavapoo, Maltipoo, Maltese, Bichonpoo, Bichon Frise, Cavapoochon, Chihuahua, Cockapoo, and Mini Dachshund are commonly approved as small breeds or crosses, though it's worth checking the full HDB-approved breed list and arranging dog licensing with us before you commit. How Every Puppy Is Checked Before You Take It Home Every puppy is health-checked before going home, and vaccinated in line with the Singapore Vaccination Guidelines for Dogs and Cats , jointly published by AVS and the Singapore Veterinary Association. Core vaccination protects against canine parvovirus and distemper, two of the most serious risks to a young puppy. The Pet Purchase Declaration: We Screen You Too Here is the part of licensing most buyers never hear about: before any sale, we are required to assess whether you are suited to own a pet. The Pet Purchase Declaration covers your housing type, whether your household agrees, and whether you realistically have the time and means for a dog. It can feel odd being on the receiving end of questions when you came to buy. But it is the single best rule in the licence: it protects the puppy from an impulsive home, and it protects you from a decision your household has not actually made. /blog/first-time-mistakes/: Home Blog First-Time Mistakes Blog · First-time owners 5 First-Time Puppy Owner Mistakes to Avoid By Nelson & Kim, Curious Tails · Published 2026-07-06 · From two years of real placements What mistakes do first-time puppy owners make? The five we see most: choosing a breed by photo instead of routine, buying a mountain of gear before understanding the puppy, breaking the night routine with 2am rescues, socialising in chaotic bursts instead of calm reps, and treating normal week-one behaviour as an emergency. All five are preventable with a simple routine and someone to call. These are not hypotheticals; they are the patterns behind two years of WhatsApp messages, delivered here in the order they usually happen. Verify our licence on the AVS public registry The five, in one card 1. Choosing by photo, not routine 2. Over-buying gear before day one 3. The 2am rescue 4. Chaotic socialisation bursts 5. Panicking at normal week-one behaviour Mistake 1: Choosing by Photo, Not Routine The costliest mistake happens before any purchase. A couple once came to us set on a Maltipoo; both work 8am to 6pm with nobody home. Maltipoos need more company than that, so we recommended a Cavapoo instead, similar look and warmth, far more independent, and risked losing the sale saying so. They took the Cavapoo. She settled beautifully into the alone-time routine, and Andrew Mak's five-star review of that steer still teaches the lesson better than we can: the right starting question is never "which breed is cutest", it is "what does our day look like?" Prevention takes two minutes: the breed selector quiz asks the routine questions in the right order. Mistake 2: Over-Buying Gear Before Day One Excited first-timers arrive at day one with three beds, a tower of toys, two food brands "for variety", and an adult-size harness the puppy will grow into around month eight. Half of it goes unused; the second food brand actively causes the week-one stomach upset it was meant to prevent. The day-one list is short and boring: playpen, bed, bowls, the same food the puppy already eats, pads, a cleaner, and two good toys. Hold the extras budget until you have lived with your actual puppy for two weeks and know what it ignores. Our puppies arrive with the 30+ item starter kit covering the whole list, which is one way to make this mistake impossible. Skip on day one Adult-size gear of any kind A second food brand "for variety" Toy mountains (two good ones win) Anything not on the short list yet Mistake 3: the 2am Rescue Night two, the whimpering starts, and somewhere around 2am the resolve breaks: the puppy is scooped into the human bed, comforted extravagantly, and taught the single clearest lesson of its young life: crying relocates me. The whimpering is adjustment, not distress; your puppy left a pile of siblings four days ago. What shortens it: a comfort toy, the pen within earshot of family life, and the same brief, boring reassurance every time. What lengthens it into months: the rescue. The full night routine, hour by hour, is in the week-by-week care guide . Mistake 4: Chaotic Socialisation Bursts The socialisation window (roughly 3 to 16 weeks) is real, and well-read owners sometimes over-correct: a Saturday crash-course of the wet market, a kids' birthday party, and a dog run, all before lunch. The puppy ends the day overwhelmed, and overwhelmed is the opposite of socialised. AVS's own guidance says it plainly: quality over quantity, positive and controlled, never forced. One calm void-deck session where the puppy watches the world from your arms beats five chaotic adventures. The AVS socialisation guidance is the reference, and the free first training lesson that comes with our puppies sets the pattern in week one. Good socialisation looks like Short, calm, positive exposures Watching from your arms counts One new thing per outing The puppy sets the pace, always Mistake 5: Panicking at Normal Week-One Behaviour Week one produces a predictable set of behaviours that read as alarming and are not: whimpering at night, an accident next to the pad rather than on it, hiding under furniture for an afternoon, one skipped meal on day one. Each has triggered a panicked 11pm message we were glad to answer. The real escalation list is short: food refused beyond a day, lethargy, vomiting, diarrhoea. Those go to a vet without delay. Everything else goes to patience, and ideally to someone who has seen a hundred week-ones and can tell you which list you are on. That someone, for our families, is our WhatsApp; and if a puppy from us falls sick in the first 5 days, it comes back to us and we nurse it. The Pattern Behind All Five Every mistake on this list is an information problem wearing a different costume: choosing blind, buying blind, comforting blind, socialising blind, panicking blind. And yet the fix is not more reading; the first-timers who thrive are rarely the best-read ones. They are the ones with a simple routine to follow and someone to call when unsure. That is the whole system, and it is buildable in a week: quiz, checklist, routine, and a number that answers. Start at the first-time owner checklist; it walks the five decisions in order. The whole system A routine to follow Someone to call when unsure That's it; that's the system First-Timer Mistake Questions 01 What is the most common first-time puppy owner mistake? Choosing the breed by photo instead of routine. Every mismatch story we have untangled in two years of placements started with a picture; the fix is answering "who is home 8am to 6pm?" before browsing a single listing. 02 Should I comfort my puppy when it cries at night? Briefly and boringly, yes; dramatically, no. The 2am rescue into the human bed teaches a lesson you will spend months unteaching. A consistent, calm response plus a comfort toy shortens the crying phase to a few nights. 03 How much gear should I buy before the puppy arrives? Less than you think. The day-one essentials fit one checklist (playpen, bed, bowls, pads, food, a couple of toys), and everything beyond it is better bought after two weeks of knowing your actual puppy. With our puppies, the 30+ item kit covers the list entirely. 04 Is week-one whimpering, hiding, or an accident an emergency? Almost never; they are adjustment behaviours that fade with routine. The genuine escalation signs are refusing food for more than a day, lethargy, vomiting, or diarrhoea; those get a vet, everything else gets consistency and patience. Still have questions? For HDB flats, the best-fit approved breeds are the Cavapoo (independent and low-shedding), the Cockapoo (the family all-rounder), the Bichonpoo and Maltipoo (low-shed companions for homes with daytime company), and the Mini Dachshund (compact character with a light-shedding smooth coat). Corgis, Shibas, and Huskies are not HDB-approved. Flat life makes three demands of a dog: cope with your work hours, keep the corridor peaceful, and not carpet the sofa in fur. The five below are ranked against exactly those demands, with the trade-offs stated out loud. The official approved list, on HDB's site Flat life's three demands 1. Cope with your alone-hours 2. Keep the corridor peaceful 3. Keep the fur off the sofa The Five Best-Fit Breeds, Ranked Honestly All five are HDB-approved and all five are published from $3,288 all-in with us. The differences are in the trade-offs. The Five Best-Fit Breeds, Ranked Honestly Breed Best for The honest trade-off 1. Cavapoo Working couples; the empty 8am-to-6pm flat Needs its grooming schedule respected; the coat mats in humidity 2. Cockapoo Families with kids; first-time owners The spaniel engine wants real 40-to-60-minute walk days 3. Mini Dachshund Character seekers; light grooming budgets A proper watchdog voice, and the back-care rules are non-negotiable 4. Bichonpoo Homes with daytime company; allergy-sensitive households Wants people around; grooming every 4 to 6 weeks 5. Maltipoo Retirees, WFH homes, constant-company households The most attachment-dependent of the five; empty weekdays are unkind to it Full profiles: Cavapoo, Cockapoo, Mini Dachshund, Bichonpoo, and Maltipoo. The Ranking Logic: Alone-Time Is the Sorter Notice what sorts the list: not cuteness, not size, but alone-time tolerance, because that is where HDB placements succeed or quietly fail. The single most common mismatch we see is a working couple choosing a companion breed that needs company all day. Cavapoos and Mini Dachshunds carry genuine independence; Maltipoos and Bichonpoos are wonderful precisely because they are attachment-driven, which becomes unkind in an empty flat. The Cockapoo sits usefully in between. If your household has someone home most days, the ranking flips: the companion crosses move to the top, and their daytime devotion becomes the feature it was always meant to be. Noise: the Real Neighbour Test The corridor question worries HDB buyers most, and the honest answer is that barking follows boredom and routine more than breed. A settled, exercised puppy of any breed here is a quiet neighbour; a bored one is not. That said, breeds have baselines: the poodle crosses announce and stop; the Mini Dachshund's watchdog voice arrives factory-installed and needs early training to stay at announcements. Both outcomes are routine problems with routine solutions, which is why the free training lesson with our puppies lands in week one. The rules themselves (one approved dog per flat, up to $4,000 for getting it wrong) are covered fully in the HDB-approved breeds guide. The Ones That Are Not Allowed (However Good the Photos) Corgis, Shiba Inus, Huskies, Golden Retrievers: none is on the HDB list, at any weight, and we say this as a shop that sells two of them. Flats cannot take them; condos and landed homes can. If the photos already got you, the honest paths are three: match the spirit inside the approved list (our Corgi and Shiba pages both map their characters to approved alternatives), treat it as a housing decision, or adopt a Singapore Special under Project ADORE. What never works: keeping one in the flat and hoping. The licence and microchip system makes every dog traceable, and the fine runs to $4,000. If someone is home most days, the Maltipoo or Bichonpoo reward that company even more; for families with kids, the Cockapoo leads. 02 Which dogs bark least in HDB flats? Barking follows boredom and routine more than breed, but among approved breeds the poodle crosses (Cavapoo, Cockapoo, Bichonpoo, Maltipoo) are announce-barkers rather than all-day protesters when properly settled. The Mini Dachshund has a bigger watchdog voice that early training keeps to announcements. 03 Are Corgis, Shibas, or Huskies allowed in HDB flats? No. None of the three is on the HDB-approved list at any weight, and workaround promises are not a plan. Condos and landed homes may keep them; flats may not. 04 Does one dog per flat really get enforced? /blog/pet-ownership-course-singapore/: Home Blog Pet Ownership Course Blog · First-time owners Pet Ownership Course Singapore: Your First Legal Step The free Pet Ownership Course is the AVS course every first-time dog owner in Singapore has to finish before a licence is issued. It runs online, takes about 20 to 30 minutes, and has been compulsory since 1 September 2024. Here is what is actually inside it, where it sits in the dog licence process, and when to do it so it never holds your puppy up. By Nelson & Kim, Curious Tails · Published 2026-07-25 · From real handover-day paperwork What is the AVS Pet Ownership Course? The Pet Ownership Course is a free online course run by Singapore's Animal and Veterinary Service (AVS). Since 1 September 2024, every first-time licence applicant for a cat or dog must complete the online Pet Ownership Course before licence issuance. It takes about 20 to 30 minutes and covers pet biology, pet care and health, responsible ownership, and the rules and legislation around owning a pet in Singapore. We complete the licensing paperwork for every puppy that leaves our shop, so we watch families meet this requirement most weeks. It is the smallest step in the whole process, and the one people worry about most. Read the AVS Pet Ownership Course page What it covers Biology: life cycle and reproduction Pet care and health: behaviour, husbandry, caring for a sick pet Responsible pet ownership Rules and legislation on owning a pet here The course, in numbers it costs nothing to take $0 it costs nothing to take minutes, start to finish 20–30 minutes, start to finish topic areas covered 4 topic areas covered time only, for first-time applicants 1 time only, for first-time applicants Where the Course Sits in the Licence Process The Pet Ownership Course is step two, not step one. The microchip comes first, because the microchip number is a required supporting document and the licence application simply cannot be submitted without it. Course second. Then the application itself, on the Pet Animal Licensing System at pals.avs.gov.sg. Several popular Singapore licensing guides list "register on PALS" as step one, which sends first-time owners to a portal they cannot finish anything on yet. Fix the order and the whole thing takes an afternoon of waiting rather than a fortnight of confusion. One date worth knowing: dogs aged three months and older must be licensed. Our puppies leave at around nine weeks, so you have a genuine runway, not a deadline breathing down your neck. The vaccination and microchipping timeline lines up with it neatly. AVS sets out the same sequence on its application steps page , including the supporting documents you will be asked for. The Four Things the Course Actually Teaches Most guides describe the syllabus as "pet care basics and licensing rules" and leave it there. AVS is more specific than that. The course covers four areas: biology, including life cycle and reproduction; pet care and health, including understanding pet behaviour, husbandry and caring for sick pets; responsible pet ownership; and the rules and legislation related to owning a pet in Singapore. The module first-time owners actually remember is the one on caring for a sick pet. Nobody plans for the 11pm scare in the first fortnight, and having heard the basics once beforehand takes the panic out of it. The legislation section is the other quietly useful one. It is where the rules that catch new owners out live, from leash requirements to the limits on how many dogs a home may keep, and it is the cheapest half hour of homework a first-time owner will ever do. The four module areas Biology: life cycle and reproduction Pet care and health: behaviour, husbandry, caring for a sick pet Responsible pet ownership Rules and legislation on owning a pet here Can You Fail It? What AVS Actually Publishes No. AVS publishes no pass mark and no fail state on its own Pet Ownership Course page. It is a set of modules to work through, not an exam with a cut-off. This is worth saying plainly, because two of the better-known Singapore licensing guides tell readers they will receive a "Certificate of Completion" and one of them puts the duration at 30 to 60 minutes. AVS says 20 to 30 minutes and says nothing about a certificate. When a commercial guide and the regulator disagree, take the regulator. What the licence application needs is that you completed the course. Nothing to memorise, nothing to revise, nothing to print and bring along. What AVS does not say No pass mark is published No fail state is published No certificate is required on the AVS page Completion is what the licence application needs How to Get In: Two Doors, Depending on Your ID AVS runs two access routes into the same course. Singpass holders use the Singpass link , and passport holders use a separate passport-holder link . The pet ownership course modules live at go.gov.sg/petownershipcourse . We mention this because it is the question we field most often from expat families, and almost nobody writing about the course online answers it. No Singpass does not mean no licence. The course is offered in all four of Singapore's official languages, and it runs perfectly well on a phone. Several of our customers have finished it on the MRT. Two ways in Singpass holders: the Singpass access link Passport holders: a separate access link All four official languages supported Works fine on a phone The One Step Your Pet Shop Cannot Do for You We complete the dog licensing and paperwork at the point of purchase, and we sit with you while it is done rather than handing over a form and wishing you luck. That is the part first-time buyers dread, and it is genuinely ours to carry. The course is the exception. It is tied to your own login and your own identity, so it has to be you, on your phone, for half an hour. There is no version of this where a shop can take it on your behalf, and any seller who offers to is telling you something about how they operate. So the honest split is a simple one: your 30 minutes, our paperwork. It is the same sentence we say at the door on handover day. When to Do It So It Never Delays Your Puppy Do the course while you are already waiting. Our puppies go home about a week after their second vaccination, which lands around week nine, and after a deposit we board the puppy free for up to a month with vaccinations continuing on schedule at our cost. That gap is measured in weeks. The course is measured in minutes. Families who leave it to collection day are the only ones we have ever seen feel rushed by it, and the rush is entirely self-inflicted. There is no processing queue and no waiting period on the course itself. Honestly, the best moment is the evening you place the deposit, while the excitement is still doing the work for you. Diary it then and it is done before the pen is even out of the box. Your actual timeline Weeks 6, 8 and 12: core vaccinations Around week 9: puppy goes home After a deposit: free boarding up to 1 month Anywhere in there: your 30 minutes What the Licence Itself Costs, and the Row Buyers Miss There is no single dog licence fee in Singapore. AVS prices in licence fee tiers, and the row nobody quotes is the one that matters most to a puppy buyer: a dog below five months of age is S$15 for a one-year licence, and that is the only duration offered at that age. Past five months the standard table takes over. A non-sterilised dog in the first three of a household is S$90 for one year, S$165 for two and S$230 for three. Sterilised rates are S$15, S$25 and S$35 for the same durations. A 10% rebate applies to payment by GIRO, online or AXS. Here is why it matters. Puppies go home unsterilised, and vets generally advise sterilisation only from around seven months, so a first licence taken late sits on the S$90 row rather than the S$15 one. Licensing at purchase, while the puppy is nine weeks old, is not just tidier. It is cheaper. Fees do get revised, so check the current AVS fee table before you pay. For the wider picture of what a first year actually costs, the first-year budget planner breaks it down line by line. Dog licence fees, by row Below 5 months: S$15, one-year only Sterilised, first 3 dogs: S$15 / S$25 / S$35 Non-sterilised, first 3 dogs: S$90 / S$165 / S$230 10% rebate via GIRO, online or AXS Rates published by AVS for the period before 1 September 2026. Verify before paying. Three Situations, Three Different Answers Buying from a licensed shop with collection weeks away? Do the course this week and forget about it. We handle the licence application at purchase, so the course is your only task on the list. Collecting in the next few days? Do it tonight. Thirty minutes now beats discovering on collection morning that the licence cannot be issued yet. Adopting or taking on a rehomed dog rather than buying? Same course, same order, but the PALS application is yours to submit, with the microchip number from whoever is passing the dog on. Every route ends at the same portal. If you are still at the stage of choosing rather than collecting, have a look at the puppies we have available first. The paperwork is easier to plan once the dog is real. Which one are you? Collecting in a few weeks: do it this week Collecting in a few days: do it tonight Adopting or rehoming: same order, your own PALS application Why This Course Exists, and Why We're Glad It Does A 30-minute gate in front of a 12 to 15 year commitment is not a burden. We would happily see it doubled. Almost every regret we have untangled in two years of matching puppies to families traces back to a decision made with no information at all: a breed picked from a photograph, a schedule nobody thought through, a seller nobody checked. None of that is stupidity. It is just how excitement works. What we tell first-time owners, though, is slightly contrarian. You do not need a lot of information upfront. You need a simple routine to follow and someone to call when you are unsure. The course gives you the baseline. The routine is what we hand over at the door, and the mistakes we spend most of our time untangling are routine problems rather than knowledge problems. The Licence That Protects You Is Not Yours Your dog licence keeps you compliant. The seller's licence is the one that protects you, and it is the check almost nobody does before paying a deposit. Every legitimate pet shop in Singapore appears on the AVS public registry, and the search takes about 60 seconds. Ours is AS24J00046. Check us first; an honest shop never minds. Unlicensed sellers are where the smuggled-puppy stories start, and a seller with no licence of their own can help you with none of the paperwork on this page. Our 60-second guide to checking any shop's licence walks the process with the red flags attached, or go straight to the AVS public registry and search a name. What Happens on Handover Day Licensing and paperwork are completed at the point of purchase, with us doing the filling in and the checking. You bring the course completion, your ID and your address, and that is the whole of your homework. The rest of the day is the good part. The starter kit, 30 or more items worth over $500, arrives with the puppy and gets set up in your home rather than left in a bag by the door, and we walk you through what every item is for. A free first lesson with an AVS-certified trainer is booked for week one. If the puppy falls sick within the first five days, bring it back and we will nurse it. After that our WhatsApp stays open for care questions for as long as you have the dog, which is the part of the service the paperwork never captures. What to bring Course completed Your ID and contact details Your home address for the licence Nothing else, we handle the rest Pet Ownership Course Questions, Answered 01 Is the AVS Pet Ownership Course really free? Yes. AVS runs it free online, and there is no paid tier or upgrade to buy. It takes about 20 to 30 minutes, which is one evening rather than one weekend. 02 Can you fail the Pet Ownership Course? AVS does not publish a pass mark or a fail state on its course page. Some third-party guides mention a certificate; AVS itself does not state one. What matters is that you complete it before you apply for the licence on PALS. 03 Do I need Singpass to do the Pet Ownership Course? No. AVS publishes two access routes, one for Singpass holders and a separate one for passport holders, so foreign residents can complete it too. The course content is the same either way. 04 Will the course delay my puppy coming home? Not if you do it during the wait. Our puppies go home about a week after their second vaccination, around week nine, and after a deposit we board them free for up to a month. Thirty minutes fits inside that gap without touching your collection date. 05 Does my pet shop handle the dog licence for me? We complete the dog licensing and paperwork at the point of purchase and walk you through every field. The one part we cannot do is the course itself, because it is tied to your own login. Your 30 minutes, our paperwork. 06 Do I need to take the course again for a second dog? The requirement is written for first-time cat or dog licence applicants, so once you already hold a licence you are no longer a first-time applicant. If your situation is unusual, check the AVS licensing requirements page rather than guessing. 07 How much is a dog licence in Singapore? It depends on which row you land on. A dog below five months old is S$15 for a one-year licence. A non-sterilised dog past that age is S$90 for one year, with two-year and three-year options priced higher. A 10% rebate applies to payment by GIRO, online or AXS. 08 What do I need before I can apply for the licence? The microchip number is the real prerequisite, because the application cannot be submitted without it. Microchip first, course second, PALS application third. /blog/puppy-fireworks-singapore/: Home Blog Puppies and fireworks Blog · Puppy care Getting Your Puppy Through NDP and New Year Fireworks By Nelson & Kim, Curious Tails · Published 2026-07-18 · Written for the first National Day with a new puppy in the house Dog scared of fireworks in Singapore? Start here A dog scared of fireworks is showing noise phobia, a normal stress response to sudden loud bangs. The plan is the same every season: give your puppy a covered safe room with the aircon on, stay calm yourself, and start gentle sound desensitisation three to four weeks before National Day. Most puppies settle far better when the loud night is not their first surprise. Below is the Singapore fireworks calendar, the safe-room setup, a week-by-week desensitisation plan, and the checklist for the night itself. If the fireworks are tonight, jump to the calm-down checklist first. Verify our licence on the AVS public registry If the fireworks are tonight Set up a quiet, covered safe room now Close the windows, curtains, aircon on Feed and toilet before it gets dark Turn on the TV or a fan for steady noise Stay calm; sit with your puppy, no fuss Why Do Fireworks Terrify Puppies? Fireworks scare puppies because the bangs are loud, sudden, and make no sense to a young dog. Puppies hear a much wider, sharper range of sound than we do, so a display that feels festive to you can feel like an attack to them. There is nothing wrong with a puppy that hides. In a Singapore high-rise it is louder still. Sound bounces between HDB blocks, rolls up from the ground, and arrives from a direction your puppy cannot see. A dog that copes fine with a passing thunderclap can come undone when the booms keep coming for twenty minutes straight. The good news: fear of fireworks is one of the most manageable problems in a puppy's first year. You cannot stop the fireworks, but you can change what they mean to your dog, and you can control the room it hears them from. Singapore's Fireworks Calendar: The Nights to Prepare For When Fireworks are tightly controlled here, so the big displays are predictable. That is your advantage. Singapore's Fireworks Calendar: The Nights to Prepare For Occasion When What to expect NDP rehearsals Saturdays through July and early August Full fireworks in the evening; often your puppy's real first exposure National Day 9 August The loudest, longest display of the year, plus flypasts New Year's Eve 31 December, midnight at Marina Bay Countdown fireworks; loud citywide if you live near the bay Festival and event nights Occasional, through the year Smaller displays and firecracker sounds around some celebrations Dates and venues shift a little each year, so check the official National Day Parade schedule and mark the rehearsal Saturdays. If you prepare for the rehearsals, the ninth of August is never the first bang your puppy hears. How Do You Build a Safe Room for a Scared Puppy? A safe room is simply the quietest interior space in your home with your puppy's playpen inside it and the outside muffled out. Pick a room away from the windows, draw the curtains, shut the windows, and turn the aircon on to soften the bangs. Most owners already have everything they need. That is the part we love: the playpen that comes in every starter kit is already your puppy's den. Add the familiar bed, a bowl of water, a favourite chew, and a worn t-shirt that smells of you. Cover part of the pen with a light blanket so it feels like a burrow. When we set up the playpen at a home delivery, we place it in the calmest corner for exactly this reason. Let your puppy choose to go in and out. Never shut it inside and walk away, because a safe room only works if it feels like shelter, not a trap. How Early Should You Start Desensitisation? Start three to four weeks before National Day. Desensitisation means teaching your puppy that firework sounds are boring and safe, one small step at a time, long before the real night arrives. Rushed in a single evening it does not work, so give it a proper runway. Here is the simple version we share with owners: Week 1: play firework or thunderstorm sounds at very low volume during meals and play, so the noise arrives alongside good things. Weeks 2 to 3: nudge the volume up a little only while your puppy stays relaxed. If it tenses, you have gone too fast; drop back a step. Every session: reward calm with a treat or gentle praise. You are pairing the bang with something good, so it starts to predict a snack, not a threat. Final week: practise in the safe room itself, so the space and the sound become a settled, familiar pair. Keep sessions short and end on a calm note. Slow and boring beats fast and frightening every time. What Do You Do on the Night Itself? On the night, get everything settled before the first bang. Feed and toilet your puppy while it is still light, ready the safe room, put steady background noise on, keep the lights low, and stay relaxed yourself. Your calm is the strongest signal your puppy has that nothing is actually wrong. The calm-down checklist we give owners: Feed dinner and do the last toilet trip before dark, before displays start. Safe room ready, curtains drawn, windows shut, aircon or a fan running. Turn on the TV, a radio, or white noise to blur the edges of the bangs. Sit with your puppy if it comes to you; speak softly, keep your body loose. Check the collar tag and that microchip details are current, in case of a bolt. If your puppy chooses to hide, let it. A dog hiding in its den is coping, not misbehaving. Your job is company and calm, not a cure in one evening. What Should You Never Do? Never punish a frightened puppy, and never force it to face the noise. Fear is not disobedience, so scolding a trembling dog only tells it that scary nights come with your anger too. Dragging it out to the balcony to watch the display does not toughen it up; it makes next year worse. The mistakes we see most, and the gentle fix for each: Scolding the fear: stay quiet and neutral instead. Calm company, not correction. Forcing exposure: let your puppy retreat to its safe room and settle at its own pace. Believing comfort spoils them: it does not. Soothing a scared puppy is fine and often helps. Leaving a first-season puppy alone: its first big display is not the night to be out. Get those four right and you have avoided the errors that turn a nervous puppy into a firework-phobic adult dog. When Is It More Than Nerves? Most puppies get a little easier each season when you prepare early and keep every experience calm. It becomes more than nerves when the panic risks harm: frantic escape attempts, injury, drooling and shaking that will not settle for hours, or a fear that clearly deepens year on year. That is the point to bring in a professional. Your vet can rule out anything medical and, for severe noise phobia, advise on anxiety aids or medication. Please do not reach for human sedatives or leftover pills; the wrong thing can leave a dog frightened and unable to move. For the training side, the free first lesson with our AVS-certified trainer is a good place to start a longer counter-conditioning plan. There is no shame in asking for help. Fireworks fear is common, and the earlier you act, the kinder each season gets. Your Puppy's First Fireworks Season A puppy that already lives by a steady daily rhythm handles a loud night far better than one that does not. The safe room you build for fireworks is the same one that helps with thunderstorms and general settling, so the effort pays off well beyond August. If your puppy is still finding its feet at home, walk through your first-weeks settling routine first. A confident, settled puppy has far less to fear when the sky starts booming. Fireworks and Your Dog: Common Questions 01 Why is my puppy so scared of fireworks? Fireworks are sudden, loud, and unpredictable, and your puppy hears them far more sharply than you do. To a young dog with no context for the noise, each bang reads as danger. It is a normal fear response, not a fault, and early preparation makes it much easier to manage. 02 When are the fireworks in Singapore I should prepare for? The two big, predictable seasons are National Day (9 August, plus the parade rehearsals on Saturdays in the weeks before it) and the New Year countdown at Marina Bay on 31 December. Check the official National Day Parade schedule each year so a rehearsal night is not your puppy's first surprise. 03 Should I comfort my dog during fireworks or ignore it? Comfort it. The old idea that soothing a scared dog rewards fear is a myth. If your puppy wants to be near you, sit with it and stay calm and quiet. What you avoid is fussing, panicking, or dragging it out to face the noise. 04 Can I still walk my puppy on a fireworks night? Do the main walk earlier in the day, well before any displays start. On National Day itself, skip the evening walk. If a last toilet trip is unavoidable, keep it short, leashed, and close to home so a sudden bang cannot send a frightened puppy bolting. 05 How far ahead of National Day should I start desensitisation? Give yourself three to four weeks. Play firework sounds at very low volume during meals and play, then raise the volume slowly only while your puppy stays relaxed. Pair every sound with treats so the bang starts to predict something good instead of something scary. 06 Will my puppy grow out of being scared of fireworks? Many puppies improve each season when you prepare early and keep every experience calm. Left unmanaged, the fear can also deepen year on year. Panic that risks injury or escape, or that will not settle for hours, is worth a conversation with your vet. Still have questions? /blog/puppy-first-night/: Home Blog First Night Home Blog · First-time owners Surviving Your Puppy's First Night at Home By Nelson & Kim, Curious Tails · Published 2026-07-19 · From real delivery-day setups What happens on a puppy's first night home? Most puppies cry for the first 20 to 40 minutes after lights-out, then settle if the playpen is set up right: pen next to your bed, a warm covered corner, a worn t-shirt with your scent, and a wee pad well away from the sleeping area. Respond to sustained crying, since it often means a toilet need, but don't rush in for every whimper, or the puppy learns crying always brings you running. This is not theory. It is the routine we walk every family through at the door, on delivery day, before we leave. Verify our licence on the AVS public registry Night one, in short Pen next to your bed, not in another room A worn t-shirt beats any $40 toy Respond to sustained crying, not every whimper No bed-sharing, even for one night What the First Night Actually Looks Like The car ride home is usually the calmest part of the day; puppies tend to sleep against a warm body. The chaos starts a few hours later, once the novelty of a new home wears off and the sun goes down. By evening, expect a burst of zoomies followed by a crash. Lights-out is when the crying usually starts, somewhere between 20 minutes and an hour after you settle them into the pen. Most puppies quiet down on their own once they realise the room is still, the family is still nearby, and nothing bad is happening. Around 2am to 4am, a genuine toilet wake-up is common for young puppies. That is different from settling-in crying, and it needs a response. Setting Up the Playpen Before You Collect the Puppy Do this before you leave to pick the puppy up, not after you get home exhausted at 9pm. Position the pen in the room you actually sleep in, ideally within arm's reach of the bed. A pen in the living room or a spare room, out of sight and smell, produces the loudest, longest crying we see. Line one corner with the bed and blanket, keep the pad and tray at the opposite end, and set water within reach but not next to the bed. Dim, not dark; a small night light helps more than most owners expect. Our 30+ item starter kit covers the whole pen setup, and we build it with you at the door on delivery day, so night one starts with the pen already right. Pen checklist before pickup Bed in the sleeping corner Pad and tray at the far end Water within reach, not by the bed Positioned in your bedroom The Scent Trick: Why a Worn T-Shirt Beats a $40 Toy Four days ago, this puppy was sleeping in a warm pile of littermates. That is the loss night one is really about, not the new house, not the new food; the missing warmth and smell of company. A t-shirt you have actually worn, unwashed, tucked into the bed corner, does more to settle a puppy than any heartbeat toy or plush on the market. It smells like a person, and a person is what the puppy is missing. Swap it for a fresh one after a few days once the puppy has bonded to your scent directly. We tell every family this at the handover, and it is the single cheapest fix in this whole guide. When to Respond to Crying, and When to Let It Ride Out Short whimpers in the first 20 to 40 minutes after lights-out are adjustment, not distress. Going in every time teaches the fastest, most durable lesson a puppy learns in its first week: crying works, every time, no exceptions. Sustained crying that doesn't taper off after several minutes is different, and especially at 2am to 4am, it is usually a genuine toilet need. AVS's own dog care guidance is consistent with what we see on delivery days: calm, consistent responses build confidence; frantic or inconsistent ones build anxiety. The AVS dog training and care guidance covers the same principle for the weeks that follow, and our free first lesson with an AVS-certified trainer builds on it directly. Respond vs ride out Short whimper, first hour: ride it out Sustained crying, 2am to 4am: check toilet Escalating panic (not just noise): check on them Quiet after checking: back into the pen The 2am Toilet Wake-Up, Without Starting a Bad Habit When the 2am cry is a genuine toilet need, keep the whole trip boring on purpose. No lights blazing, no play, no baby voice, no cuddle session. Carry the puppy straight to the pad or outside, wait, then straight back into the pen. Exciting 2am trips teach a puppy that waking up is fun, which turns one toilet break into a nightly play session within a week. Boring trips teach the opposite: toilet, then back to sleep, nothing more happens. This single habit, kept boring from night one, is usually the difference between a puppy sleeping through by week three and one still waking the household at month two. What Not to Do on Night One Bed-sharing is the big one. It feels like the kind thing to do at 3am, and it is also the fastest way to create a dog that cannot sleep alone at all by month two, which then needs weeks of separate, harder retraining to undo. Room-hopping is the second trap: moving the pen to wherever the crying stops that night. Pick one spot before pickup day and keep it there for at least the first two weeks, even on the rough nights. And don't punish the crying. It is not defiance; it is a four-month-old animal that lost its entire family four days ago. Calm and consistent beats stern every time. How Night One Sets the Pattern for Week One Families who keep the pen fixed, the trips boring, and the responses calm are usually through the crying phase within three to five nights. Families who bend the rules on night one, understandably, in the moment, tend to still be negotiating with a puppy at 2am two weeks later. None of this needs to be figured out alone. If a puppy from us falls sick within the first 5 days, it comes straight back to us and we nurse it; and for the routine questions, WhatsApp is open every day we're not asleep either. The fuller week-by-week routine, including feeding and toilet-training schedules, is in the puppy care 101 guide . First Night Home Questions 01 How long does a puppy cry on the first night? Most puppies settle within 20 to 40 minutes of lights-out once the playpen is set up right: warm corner, worn t-shirt with your scent, pad away from the sleeping area. A few keep going longer, especially if the pen is in an unfamiliar room away from the family. 02 Should I let my puppy sleep in bed with me on the first night? No. It feels kind in the moment, but it teaches the puppy that crying gets it a spot in your bed, a habit that takes far longer to undo than the one restless night it was meant to fix. Keep the pen close to your bed instead, not in it. 03 Where should the playpen go on night one? Next to your bed, or in the room you sleep in. A puppy alone in another room cries longer and louder because it can't see or smell anyone. Within earshot and eyeshot is the whole trick. 04 What if my puppy wakes up crying at 2am? Check for a toilet need first; a young puppy genuinely can't hold it all night. Take them out calmly, no play, no fuss, then straight back into the pen. Sustained crying with no toilet need usually settles on its own within a few minutes if you don't rush in every time. 05 Is it normal for a puppy to refuse food on the first night? Yes, a skipped first meal is common and not a concern on its own. It becomes a concern only if it stretches past a full day, or comes with lethargy, vomiting, or diarrhoea; those get a vet call. HDB flats may keep one dog, and it must be from HDB's approved list of around 62 small breeds and their crosses, such as the Bichon Frise, Toy Poodle, Maltese, Miniature Dachshund, and Chihuahua. Non-approved breeds like Corgis, Shiba Inus, and Golden Retrievers are not allowed in flats, and non-compliance can draw a fine of up to $4,000. Day 0: arrive into a ready playpen, explore at its own pace, first meal on the usual food. Days 1 to 3: fixed meal times, a consistent toilet spot, calm handling, some night whimpering. Days 4 to 7: the routine starts holding, the first training lesson happens, and gentle carried socialisation begins. Boring, on purpose. A new puppy runs on routine: fixed feeding, one toilet spot, a playpen it owns, calm nights, and gentle socialisation inside the 3-to-16-week window. Everything below is that sentence, expanded and localised to Singapore. Verify our licence on the AVS public registry The five anchors Fixed meal times (three a day) One consistent toilet spot A playpen the puppy owns A calm, repeatable bedtime Gentle socialisation, 3 to 16 weeks Day One, Hour by Hour Hour 0: your puppy explores the playpen at its own pace, no welcome party, no passing-around. If we delivered, the pen is already set up and smells of its own bed, which is exactly why we set up before letting the puppy out; see how delivery day works. Hour 2 or so: first meal, the same food it has been eating, water always available. First toilet trip to the pad right after; success gets quiet praise, misses get cleaned without comment. Evening: dim the lights, keep voices low, and let the day be boring. Everything your puppy needs on day one is in the starter kit, and everything you need is patience. Week One: Feeding on the Clock Three meals a day, at the same times every day, of the same food your puppy arrived with. Diet continuity is the single biggest protector of week-one digestion, and week-one digestion is the single biggest protector of toilet training. Portion by the food's small-breed guide, not by the eyes looking up at you. If you eventually want a different brand, transition over a week or so, a quarter at a time. Meals also power the toilet routine: puppies go after eating with near-clockwork reliability, so each mealtime ends with a trip to the pad. That is the whole system. Week One: Nights, Whimpering, and the Comfort Toy The first two or three nights usually include whimpering, and here is the truth that saves families: it is adjustment, not distress. Your puppy slept in a pile of siblings last week; alone is new. What shortens it: a comfort toy in the bed, the pen where the family's evening sounds still reach, and a calm, consistent response, the same brief reassurance every time. What lengthens it: dramatic rescues into the human bed at 2am, which teach exactly the lesson you'd expect. By night four or five, most puppies sleep through. If yours doesn't, WhatsApp us; the fix is usually one detail. Week one is when the free lesson lands Every puppy of ours includes a first lesson with an AVS-certified trainer, booked into week one while the routine is forming. See the free lesson Weeks 2 to 4: the Socialisation Window Is Open Between roughly 3 and 16 weeks of age, new experiences register as normal instead of alarming, and that window is open right now. AVS's own guidance is the standard we follow: positive, controlled exposure to people, sounds, surfaces, and calm vaccinated dogs, with quality beating quantity every time. Until the week-12 vaccination clears ground walks in busy areas, carry your puppy: a carried tour of the void deck, the lift lobby, and the corridor at different hours covers traffic sounds, strangers, and lift chimes safely. One rule from the AVS socialisation guidance worth engraving: never force an interaction. A puppy that watches from your arms is socialising; a puppy that gets passed to every enthusiastic stranger is not. The Vaccination and Licensing Timeline Singapore's schedule, in exact weeks. If your puppy is from us, the first two rows are already done at homecoming. The Singapore-Specific Parts Heat first: walk before 9am and after 6pm, full stop. Midday pavement here burns small paws, and a puppy will not tell you until it has. The five-second rule works: if the back of your hand cannot rest on the pavement for five seconds, neither can paws. Haze weeks and monsoon afternoons happen; a corridor of fetch, ten minutes of kibble-scatter sniffing, and a stuffed chew toy will honestly retire a small puppy indoors. Exercise is about the brain as much as the legs at this age. And HDB corridor noise: lift chimes, renovation drilling, neighbours' slippers. Treat each as a socialisation rep, not an annoyance; a puppy that hears drilling from its calm playpen at 10 weeks ignores it for life. Ongoing costs for all of this are in the first-year budget planner. An AVS-Accredited Certified Dog Trainer (ACDT) is a trainer accredited under the scheme the Animal and Veterinary Service launched on 10 December 2022 as Singapore's benchmark for dog-training competency. Accreditation requires certification from recognised international animal behaviour organisations and a commitment to rewards-based, science-backed methods. It covers settling your puppy into its playpen routine, a potty routine that actually works with your floor plan and schedule, and handling basics: how to hold the leash, how to reward, how to end a session before the puppy tips into overtired chaos. Half of the lesson is really for you. Puppies learn fast; the routine only sticks if the humans are consistent, so the trainer coaches your technique as much as the puppy's behaviour. The lesson provides the routine; the starter-kit walkthrough at delivery covers the equipment; our WhatsApp covers the someone. Why Week One Matters: the Socialisation Window Puppies have a critical socialisation window between roughly 3 and 16 weeks of age. Inside it, new people, sounds, surfaces, and calm vaccinated dogs register as normal; after it closes, the same experiences take far more work to accept. That is AVS's own guidance, and it is why we push the free lesson into week one instead of "whenever you get around to it". The guidance comes with two caveats worth repeating: quality over quantity (a few positive, controlled exposures beat a chaotic market walk), and socialisation is a lifelong process, not a box ticked at 16 weeks. For the day-by-day version of week one, feeding times and all, see the week-by-week puppy care guide, and the AVS dog training and socialisation guidance for the source material. Rewards-Based, Because It Works The method behind the lesson is rewards-based training: mark the behaviour you want, pay it with a treat or play, and ignore or redirect the rest. AVS describes it as supported by decades of scientific research and recommended by veterinary and animal behaviour organisations worldwide, and made it the benchmark of the ACDT scheme for a reason. It also happens to be the method a first-time owner can actually execute. Corrections require timing and confidence most new owners do not have yet; rewarding a sit requires a treat pouch. For a small breed in an HDB flat, that matters twice over: a puppy trained through trust barks less, settles faster, and treats its playpen as territory rather than punishment. Core vaccinations at weeks 6, 8, and 12, with an optional fourth at week 16 if the vet advises it. Deworming happens together with every vaccination visit. Puppies go home about a week after the second vaccination, around week 9, and the booster is annual from year one onward. That paragraph settles most arguments with confusing schedules online. Singapore Vaccination Guidelines for Dogs and Cats The schedule, memorised Weeks 6, 8, 12: core vaccinations Week 16: optional fourth, vet's call Deworming with every visit Home around week 9 Annual booster from year 1 The Full Timeline : Vaccinations, Microchip, Licence Health and paperwork on one timeline, because in Singapore they interlock. The Full Timeline: Vaccinations, Microchip, Licence When What happens Week 6 First core vaccination and deworming Week 8 Second core vaccination and deworming Week 9 Homecoming: about one week after the second vaccination Week 12 Third core vaccination and deworming; completes the puppy course Week 16 Optional fourth vaccination, if your vet advises it Year 1 onward Annual booster and deworming, every year Before homecoming Microchipping (mandatory) is done At purchase Dog licensing completed; first-time owners do the free online pet ownership course Authority sources: the Singapore Vaccination Guidelines for Dogs and Cats , AVS licensing requirements , and the pet ownership course for first-time owners. Why Homecoming Is Week 9, Not Earlier The week-9 timing is logic, not tradition: the second vaccination lands at week 8, and protection needs about a week to build before the puppy takes on the immune stress of moving home, new sounds, new food and water, new everything. Which makes early availability a diagnostic: a seller offering a 6- or 7-week-old puppy "ready today" is either skipping shots or skipping the wait, and both mean the same corner got cut. The polite question that reveals it: "which vaccinations has this puppy had, and when?" It is also why we board reserved puppies free until they are genuinely ready; the schedule sets homecoming, not the invoice. Smuggled puppies are brought into Singapore across the border, typically from Malaysia, without vaccinations, health checks, or legal channels, and sold through Carousell, Telegram, or Facebook at prices below the licensed market. The documented consequences: puppies dying of parvovirus in transit, treatment bills of $5,000 to $10,000 for survivors, and since 2026, buyers themselves prosecuted. This page exists to keep you out of those stories, not to frighten you with them. Four documented cases, the economics that create the 'bargains', and the 60-second check that settles everything. Nothing here is embellished; it doesn't need to be. Four Cases, All Documented Case What happened The outcome Tuas checkpoint, 2024 12 puppies found in a modified car boot compartment Puppies died of canine parvovirus; the case became the reference image of what "no paperwork" means Pomeranian smuggling, 2023 5 Pomeranian puppies in a plastic container in a car boot All 5 tested positive for parvovirus; the smuggler was jailed 16 weeks 26 puppies and a cat, 2023 A single smuggling run of 26 puppies 1 dead on arrival, 18 died of parvovirus after; 12 months' jail The buyer prosecution, 2026 A man bought a smuggled puppy, unknowingly by his account Fined $7,000 in the first NParks prosecution of a purchaser; buyers are now liable too Sources: CNA on the Tuas case , the Straits Times on the Pomeranian case , Mothership on the 26-puppy run , and the Straits Times on the buyer's $7,000 fine . The Economics: Why the 'Bargain' Exists An unlicensed puppy runs $500 to $1,000 below the licensed market, and the discount has a source: it is the exact cost of everything that was skipped. No vaccinations at weeks 6 and 8, no vet checks, no deworming, no microchip, no licensed premises with welfare inspections. The price is low because the puppy arrived in a car boot instead of through any of that. The buyer inherits the skipped costs with interest. Parvovirus treatment runs $5,000 to $10,000, survival is not guaranteed, and the emotional cost of a week-one hospitalisation does not appear on any invoice. Two years inside the licensed side of this industry taught us the blunt version: a cheaper puppy from an unlicensed source is not a bargain; it is a financial and emotional risk priced to look like one. The Liability Shift: Buyers Now Answer Too For years, enforcement landed on smugglers and sellers. The 2026 case changed the arithmetic: NParks prosecuted the purchaser, and the court fined him $7,000, in a case reported as the first of its kind. The practical meaning for you: "I didn't know" is not a defence you want to test, and you never have to. The AVS registry check takes 60 seconds and settles whether a seller is legitimate before any money moves; run it and buyer liability simply never reaches you. The full check, red flags included, is in our step-by-step licence verification guide. The remaining gap is demand, and that is where you come in: every buyer who runs the registry check either buys licensed or walks away, and both outcomes shrink this market. Welfare groups like the SPCA have campaigned on this for years ; the buyer-side check is the piece individuals control. What the licensed path looks like, priced and itemised, is on our transparent pricing page; the $500-to-$1,000 "premium" buys everything the car boot skipped. Not necessarily; registries list registered business entities, and a shop's marketing name can differ from its registered name. Ask the shop for its licence number and search that instead. A legitimate shop hands the number over instantly; refusal or evasion is the actual red flag. 03 Does "licensed" mean the puppies are guaranteed healthy? It means the shop is subject to welfare inspections, must screen buyers through the Pet Purchase Declaration, and must meet health, vaccination, and microchipping requirements. That is a strong floor, not a magic guarantee; still read the individual puppy's paperwork. 04 What should I do if a seller is not listed? Walk away and transfer nothing, however good the price looks. Buyers have been fined $7,000 over smuggled dogs, so an unlisted seller is your legal risk too, not just the puppy's. Suspicious listings can be reported to AVS. 05 Can I practise the check on a real shop? Yes: search AS24J00046, our licence, on the registry. That is exactly what a passing result looks like, and running it on us first is precisely the habit this page is trying to build. Still have questions? What Actually Drives a Puppy's Price Four things move a puppy's price in Singapore: breed demand against how few litters are available locally, adult size, coat type and colour, and age at sale. A wavy-coated small cross in a popular colour will always sit above a common coat, because more families are queuing for the same few puppies. The fifth driver is the one listings never mention: what it costs to sell a puppy legally. A licensed shop carries AVS licensing, proper housing, vet checks, vaccinations, and microchipping before any puppy goes home, and those costs sit inside every honest price. This page explains what that means in practice, in line with Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA). What we collect When you contact us on WhatsApp, by phone, or by email, we receive the details you share with us: your name, contact number, and anything you tell us about your home and lifestyle so we can recommend a suitable breed. When you buy a puppy, we collect the details required to complete AVS licensing, microchip registration, and the Pet Purchase Declaration — this is a regulatory requirement for every licensed pet shop in Singapore. Our website itself does not require an account and has no login. If we enable analytics (Google Analytics 4), it collects standard usage data such as pages visited and approximate location, using cookies. How we use it To answer your enquiry, match you with a suitable puppy, arrange delivery and your free training lesson, and provide after-sale support. To meet our legal obligations as an AVS-licensed pet shop, including dog licensing and microchip records. We do not sell your personal data, and we do not send marketing you have not asked for. Third-party services WhatsApp (Meta) handles chat messages you send us — their own privacy policy applies to the WhatsApp service. Google services on this site include an embedded Google Map of our Balestier shop and, if enabled, Google Analytics. These may set cookies governed by Google’s privacy policy. Regulatory data (licensing, microchip) is shared with AVS/NParks as required by law. Retention and protection We keep enquiry messages only as long as needed to help you, and purchase records for as long as Singapore law and AVS licensing conditions require. Access to customer information is limited to Nelson and Kim, the owners who run Curious Tails day to day. Your rights under the PDPA Under Singapore’s Personal Data Protection Act, you may ask us what personal data we hold about you, ask us to correct it, or withdraw consent for its use (subject to legal retention requirements). The honest footnotes, and this breed has real ones. First, the Beagle is a pack hound that hates being alone; it wants company and, ideally, a busy household. Second, it is food-obsessed to a fault, which is a gift for training and a hazard for waistlines and bins. Third, it is independent and scent-driven, so training takes patience and a sense of humour: this is not a Border Collie waiting on your every word. Fourth, see the nose-and-voice section next, because those two traits define daily life with a Beagle. Can a Beagle Be Left Alone During Work Hours? Not happily, and this is the honest heart of the breed. Beagles are pack animals that struggle with long solitude, and a lonely, bored Beagle is exactly the one that bays, howls and empties the bin. They do best in busy homes where someone is around much of the day, or with a midday walker and a dog-savvy routine. The room needs the usual tropical basics — ventilation, shade, water — plus food-puzzle toys to occupy that nose, and the exercise contract below decides the rest. Good fit if Private housing and a busy, present family You accept a vocal, scent-driven hound Someone is around much of the day, or a midday walker The Nose and the Voice: What Every Beagle Owner Lives Two traits define this breed, and no honest page hides them. The nose first: the Beagle has one of the finest noses in the dog world, and it rules the dog. On a scent, a Beagle can go temporarily deaf to its own name, which is why it is a leash-first dog in any open space, why your garden must be genuinely secure, and why a food-driven training approach works far better than expecting obedience to beat an interesting smell. Channel the nose with scent games and puzzle feeders and you have a happy, tired dog. The voice second: Beagles were bred to bay across open country, and they can be loud. A well-exercised, well-trained Beagle in a busy home is much quieter than the stereotype, but the potential is there, and in a condo with shared walls it is a genuine factor to weigh honestly before you buy. We would rather you plan for the voice than be surprised by it, and we will talk you through managing it. Beagle Size , Coat and Lifespan Honest numbers for a compact, sturdy scent hound.
